turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Doctor. I'm here because... well, I just can't stop seeing this droop and unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It's all I can look at in every single photo and reflection. 

Even when people tell me I look fine, it just feels so obvious to me. It's actually gotten to the point where I've started avoiding presentations at work, and I'm even backing out of meeting with my clients. I just don't want anyone looking at me.

turns.doctor_question: Have you seen a doctor or dermatologist about this concern with your mouth and jaw, or have you considered any cosmetic procedures to address it?

turns.doctor_question: Have you repeatedly asked friends, family members, or anyone else to look at your mouth and jaw or to reassure you about whether it looks abnormal?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, I do. I ask my husband constantly if my face looks lopsided. But it really goes beyond just asking him. 

Before work or... well, really any family event, I can spend hours just checking the bathroom mirror. I take pictures on my phone from all these different angles to see how bad the droop is. I'll redo my makeup over and over, or try to adjust my scarf to hide my jawline. And then I usually end up scrolling through photos of other women online, just to see how bad my face looks compared to theirs. It just takes up so much of my time.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes engaging in extensive appearance-related repetitive behaviors, including excessive mirror checking, reassurance seeking from her husband, camouflaging with makeup and a scarf, and comparing herself to photos of other women.

turns.doctor_question: When your husband looks at your mouth and jaw, what does he actually say? Does he tell you that he can see the droop and unevenness that you're describing, or does he say he doesn't notice anything wrong?
